### Chapter XXXV.
### Of the divine Use of the Stone

I do not see what a man, who by the blessing of God, will have perfectly accomplished this work, has to wish for in this world after that, if not that he may, in all liberty, and without fearing the deceptions and the malice of the wicked, serve and honor his God all his life. For it would be a vanity altogether unbearable if a person to whom God had granted such a great grace had the ambition to appear with pomp and brilliance in the world, to make himself admired. No, believe me, those who have this science are very far from having such thoughts: on the contrary, there is nothing they despise more.
But here is what the happiness and the felicity is of him to whom God has wished to give this talent.
Firstly, if he lived a thousand years, and he had every day a thousand thousand men to feed and maintain, he would never lack anything for that.

De hac ave dicit Plinius, licet probabile non sit, quod posterius ab ovo egreditur: quod si verum est, causa eius esse non potest nisi capitis ponderositas et magnitudo, propter quam caput ipsum diu declinat et immobile manet: posterius autem parvum est et curtum, ac si avis ipsa sit decurtata.

Est autem avis haec curvorum unguium et acuti et curvi rostri sicut sunt ungues et rostra fere omnium avium rapacium, et est varia in plumis et maioris quantitatis inter eas quae nocte valent.

15. Buteus vocatur avis rapax subnigra quam Germanice brobuxen vocamus, et est pigri volatus et uncorum unguium et curvi rostri fere quantitatis milvi. Venatur autem ranas et mures et aviculas pigras aut infirmas volare non valentes et rapit pullos avium aliquando, et est ad comedendum dulcissima et saporosa si decoctione optesis praeparata fuerit.

16. Butorius avis est similis ardeae in figura et quantitate, sed colore dissimilis quia videtur butorius esse similis terrae. Collum autem habet longum et hoc intrahit curvando et extrahit extendendo sicut ardea et venatione piscium vivit: et ideo crura longa sortita est ut circa ripas et litora venari possit. Haec adeo immobilis stat quando venatur, ut putetur mortua vel res esse inanimata: et cum illaqueatam se sentit, stat immobilis et venatorem se accipientem incautum et impraemeditatum vulnerat rostro in quo multum valet sicut et ardea. Haec avis miri odoris est cum assatur, et sanguis eius multum confert guttosis. Haec etiam avis tempore veris quando luxuriandum est, horride strepit sicut cum cornu et hoc facere non praevalet nisi quando rostrum luto aquoso immittit, ut vox in ipso rumpatur ad modum tonitrui.

17. Bistarda avis est bis vel ter saltum dans antequam terra sublevari possit: et ideo ex re nomen accepit.

Haec in quantitate et figura est ut aquila, curvo rostro et unguibus aduncis, sed in alis et cauda alba est et in cetero corpore varia ut aquila, carnibus vescitur, sed volatilia non praedatur, sed vel cadavera forte inventa comedit vel animal innocens ut agnum vel lepusculum occidit, nec haec sola perficit, sed pluribus harum avium congregatis, ausum invasionis accipiunt. Herbas etiam quando famescit comedit, et in herba ciceris et pisae et leguminum plus delectatur: quod rarum est de avibus quae carne vescuntur. Propter tarditatem in alto nidum non collocat, sed in terra ovat tempore quando seges maturatur.

Pliny says of this bird, although it is not probable, that it emerges from the egg backwards. If this is true, the cause can only be the weight and size of its head, because of which the head itself declines for a long time and remains immobile. The rear, however, is small and short, as if the bird itself were truncated.

This bird has curved claws and a sharp, curved beak, as are the claws and beaks of almost all birds of prey. It is variegated in feathers and of a larger size among those that hunt by night.

15. The <term>Buteus</term> <gloss>buzzard</gloss> is called a bird of prey, somewhat black, which in German we call *brobuxen*. It is of sluggish flight, with hooked claws and a curved beak, of nearly the size of a kite. It hunts frogs, mice, and small, sluggish birds, or those that are infirm and unable to fly, and sometimes it seizes the chicks of birds. It is very sweet and flavorful for eating if it has been prepared by boiling.

16. The <term>Butorius</term> <gloss>bittern</gloss> is a bird similar to the heron in figure and size, but different in color because the bittern appears similar to the earth. It has a long neck, which it draws in by curving and stretches out by extending, just as the heron, and it lives by hunting fish. For this reason, it has been granted long legs so that it can hunt around banks and shores. This bird stands so immobile when it hunts that it is thought to be dead or an inanimate thing. When it feels itself ensnared, it stands immobile, and if the hunter takes it incautiously or without premeditation, it wounds him with its beak, in which it is very strong, just like the heron. This bird has a wonderful odor when it is roasted, and its blood contributes much to the gouty. This bird also makes a horrible sound in the spring when it is to be in rut, like a horn, and it cannot do this unless it inserts its beak into muddy water, so that the sound is broken in the water in the manner of thunder.

17. The <term>Bistarda</term> <gloss>bustard</gloss> is a bird that takes a leap twice or three times before it can be lifted from the earth, and for this reason, it received its name from the act <note>Latin: *bis tardare*, "to delay twice"</note>.

In size and figure, it is like an eagle, with a curved beak and hooked claws, but it is white in the wings and tail, and in the rest of its body, it is variegated like an eagle. It feeds on flesh, but it does not prey on birds; rather, it eats carcasses found by chance or kills an innocent animal, such as a lamb or a small hare. It does not accomplish this alone, but when several of these birds gather, they take the courage for an invasion. When it is hungry, it also eats herbs, and it takes more delight in the herbs of chickpeas, peas, and legumes, which is rare for birds that feed on flesh. Because of its slowness, it does not place its nest in a high place but lays eggs on the ground at the time when the crops are ripened.

съ тѣмъ исправленнымъ въ Петербургѣ текстомъ, о которомъ Гоголь сообщалъ Щекину 29 апрѣля 1836 года, приходимъ къ заключенію, что послѣдняя петербургская редакція „Женитьбы“ была совершенно переработана въ Римѣ. Передѣлка піесы производилась по частямъ, отдѣльными набросками, о характерѣ которыхъ могутъ намъ дать понятіе немногіе изъ уцѣлѣвшихъ, приведенные нами выше. Имя невѣсты не установлено твердо: она называется то Агаѳья Тихоновна, то Агаѳья Петровна (ср. ниже, въ варіантахъ — 3-е и 4-е прим. къ 358 стр., 15-е примѣчаніе къ 361 стр.). Въ февральской книжкѣ „Москвитянина“ на 1841 г. (ч. I, смѣсь, стр. 616) Погодинъ извѣстилъ читателей своего журнала, что „комедія Женихъ въ двухъ дѣйствіяхъ давно готова“. Это извѣстіе относится, вѣроятно, къ той римской редакціи „Женитьбы“, которая переписана была набѣло Пановымъ и Гоголемъ въ указанную нами рукопись (ИМ.). Авторъ не считалъ однако піесы въ этомъ видѣ „готовою“. Въ Римѣ же онъ и приступилъ къ ея окончательной отдѣлкѣ. Сверху бѣловаго текста Гоголь началъ приписывать поправки и дополненія къ нему; они наносились сначала чернилами, позднѣе карандашомъ. Послѣднія, т. е. карандашныя поправки встрѣчаются преимущественно во второй тетради (стр. 23—46)¹. Поправки чернилами нанесены ранѣе карандашныхъ; чернила, которыми онѣ сдѣланы, черныя; текстъ писанъ другими чернилами — желтоватыми. Впрочемъ, тѣ и другія поправки не особенно крупны и многочисленны; онѣ-то и дали печатной редакціи „Женитьбы“ тотъ видъ, который отличаетъ ее отъ первоначальнаго бѣловаго текста римской редакціи піесы. Всѣ эти поправки указаны ниже въ варіантахъ.

При окончательной „перечисткѣ“ римской редакціи комедіи, для печати, Гоголь замѣтилъ, что при перепискѣ піесы набѣло онъ, по недосмотру, пропустилъ почти все четвертое явленіе втораго дѣйствія. Въ римской рукописи „Женитьбы“ страница 52-я оканчивалась словами: „Видя прочихъ, испускаетъ“; слѣдующая же страница начинается явленіемъ пятымъ. Пропущенное мѣсто переписано было Гоголемъ собственноручно на четверткѣ обыкновенной писчей бумаги русской фабрики. Вѣроятно, это дополненіе къ римской редакціи „Женитьбы“ было написано во время пребыванія Гоголя въ Россіи, съ октября 1841 г. до половины мая.

¹ Эта тетрадь начинается слѣдующимъ мѣстомъ 13 явленія: «Ѳекла Ивановна. Есть, есть, дай только прежде съ духомъ собраться» (стр. 367); оканчивается: «Ну, этого только мнѣ и нужно. (Оба уходятъ)». Ср. выше, стр. 382.

with the text corrected in Petersburg, about which Gogol informed Shchekin on April 29, 1836, we come to the conclusion that the latter Petersburg version of "Marriage" was completely reworked in Rome. The revision of the play was carried out in parts, in separate drafts, the character of which can be grasped from the few surviving ones we have cited above. The name of the bride is not firmly established: she is called sometimes Agafya Tikhonovna, sometimes Agafya Petrovna (cf. below, in the variants — 3rd and 4th notes to page 358, 15th note to page 361). In the February issue of *Moskvityanin* for 1841 (Part I, Miscellany, p. 616), Pogodin informed the readers of his journal that "the comedy 'The Suitor' in two acts has long been ready." This news likely refers to that Roman version of "Marriage" which was transcribed into the manuscript (IM) indicated by us by Panov and Gogol. The author, however, did not consider the play "ready" in this form. It was in Rome that he began its final finishing. Over the fair copy, Gogol began to add corrections and supplements; they were applied first in ink, later in pencil. The latter, i.e., the pencil corrections, are encountered predominantly in the second notebook (pp. 23—46)¹. The ink corrections were applied earlier than the pencil ones; the ink with which they were made is black; the text was written with other ink — yellowish. However, both those and other corrections are not particularly large or numerous; they are what gave the printed version of "Marriage" the form that distinguishes it from the original fair copy of the Roman version of the play. All these corrections are indicated below in the variants.

During the final "clean copy" of the Roman version of the comedy for printing, Gogol noticed that, when transcribing the play into a fair copy, he had, through oversight, skipped almost the entire fourth scene of the second act. In the Roman manuscript of "Marriage," page 52 ended with the words: "Seeing the others, he emits"; the following page begins with scene five. The omitted passage was copied by Gogol in his own hand on a quarter-sheet of ordinary writing paper from a Russian factory. It is likely that this addition to the Roman version of "Marriage" was written during Gogol's stay in Russia, from October 1841 until the middle of May 1842. The text begins on this quarter-sheet with the words: "an exclamation and bows"; it ends: "No, I won't slip away! By God, I won't slip away!"¹ Gogol took this scrap with him abroad.

¹ This notebook begins with the following passage from scene 13: "Fekla Ivanovna. There is, there is, just let me catch my breath first" (p. 367); it ends: "Well, that is just what I need. (Both leave)." Cf. above, p. 382.

The Catholic Church is a gathering of men inwardly called, and grafted into Christ by faith, according to the eternal foreknowledge and predestination of God; called, I say, to justification and glorification. The third, concerning the speech of Zacharias, by which he declares that he was not sufficiently moved to believe the words of the Angel. The fourth comprises the Angel's second address, by which he establishes faith in his words and punishes the incredulity of Zacharias with an evident sign. We shall treat these with what brevity we can.

He diligently notes the apparition of the Angel, expressing the time, the place, and the manner of the apparition. To the time pertains what he says, <term>en tō hierateuein auton, en tē taxei tēs ephēmerias autou</term> <gloss>while he executed the priest's office, in the order of his course</gloss>. For the fact that the Angel appears to Zacharias while he is established in his office indicates that he had been in office up to that point, and had been lacking such an apparition during his leisure time outside of his office, up until this hour of the reign of Herod.

deviate toward the extremes. For some verge toward the hot, others toward the cold, others toward the dry, others toward the moist; some toward the hot and moist, and the rest in like manner tend toward the extremes of the latitude, more or less according to the portion of the dominant element, as was declared before. From these, it is clear that there are infinite temperaments differing in the ratio of greater and lesser, of which each one assumes a portion of that latitude. But perhaps we discuss these matters more copiously than pertains to the present subject. Let us therefore return to the plan. Since, therefore, the temperaments of man are born from the elements, the books on the elements are followed by three on the temperaments. The first two of these, as Galen says, treat of the temperament of living beings, and the third of the temperament of medicines. These are followed by the book on the faculties of simple medicines, without which they cannot easily be understood. After the two books on the temperaments, the short work on unequal intemperance should be read, so that it may be known upon what these things immediately depend. However, since it is not possible to understand whether a body is best constituted and in a good habit, or the contrary, without a discussion of the temperaments, two short books follow: one on the best constitution of the body, and the other on a good habit, although the work on the natural faculties can precede this. 
<note>The term <term>temperamentum</term> <gloss>tempered state/mixture</gloss> refers to the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, dry, and moist—within a body.</note>

Budæus, ut etiam monet doctiſſimus Constantinus, <term>κρεμάδρας</term> legit. <term>Κρεμάδρα</term> vas aſſervandis obſoniorum reliquiis deſtinatū, quod penſile repoſitorium rectè dixeris. Scholiaſtes <term>τοῦτο τὸ σκεῦος εἰς ὁ τὰ σιτίδια ὀ ψα ἑκάστοτε ἀποτίθεασι, διὰ τὸ μετέωρον εἶναι καὶ κρεμάμενον. κρέμαστra κρεμάθρα</term>. Aſtronomica & Geometrica inſtrumenta penſilia ſunt, ut docet interpres Aristoph. in illud in Nebulis. <term>τιπύπιος γὰρ ἴσ’ ἐπὶ καὶ τῶν κρεμαθρῶν, ἃ ἱρίσει, τῶν εὐζώδι</term>. Sed apud Theophrastum, ut monet doctiſſ. Constantinus, ſignificat, multifidum pediculum, quo fructus appenduntur, flores extremis ramis, ſingulari appendice, racematī cohærent, albi, una parte qua ſoli obverſi ſunt, nonnihil purpuraſcentes, concavi, lilium convallium floribus perſimiles. Sunt hi parvi, rotundi, hiantes, per oras denticulati ac reflexi.

<margin>Κάρνειος Δῶρικος.</margin>
Vertunt vel carnius Doricus ; quid ſit carnius Doricus neſcio. Suidas festum quoddam eſſe ſcribit. <term>κήρειος ἀπόλλων, κήρνια ἀπόλλωνος ἑορτὴ ἐν Λακεδαιμονίοις</term>. hoc nihil ad arbutum. Scribe, <term>κεράνιον δοκανὸν</term>, capitellum Doricum, vel, <term>κιονόκρανον</term>, vel <term>κεράνιον τοῦ Δωρικοῦ κίονος</term>, ſummitas vel caput columnæ Doricæ. Epiſtylium vocat Vitruvius & capitellum, apud Pollucem <term>κιονόκρανα, καὶ κεφαλαὶ τῶν κίονων</term>. Capitello columnæ non ineptè flos deciduus comparari poteſt.

<term>Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς</term>. Hæc Plinius in hunc reddidit ſenſum. Fructus anno matureſcit paritérque floret ſubnaſcens, & prior cogitur, (lego ex antiquo codice coquitur, id eſt, matureſcit, ut Botanici loquuntur.) Mas ſit an fœmina ſterilis, inter auctores non convenit. Miror Theoph. fructum non delineaſſe. De eo hæc refert Dioſcorides <term>καρπὸς ἔχων ὡς κηκυμήλου μέγεθος, ἀπύρηνον μιμαίκυλον</term> (ita legendum ſupra docuimus) <term>κιχλίδιον, πεπανοῦθαι δὲ ὑπόκιρρον ἢ ἐρυθρὸν, ἰδιόδωρον ἀχυρώδης, κακοστόμαχον καὶ κεφαλαλγῆ</term>. (Scribe <term>ἀχυρώδη</term>, ſi non & hoc verbum corrumptur & <term>κεφαλαλγῆ</term>: nam ad <term>κομάρου καρπόν</term>, hoc est, arbuti fructum verba hæc referenda ſunt.) fructum proferens, pruni magnitudine, nuclei expertem, cui mimaiculo cognomen eſt, quique ubi mature-

<column-break/>

ſcit ſubfulvus, aut rubicundus conſpicitur, in eſu aceroſus, ſtomacho is adverſatur, capitiſque dolorem excitat. Vox <term>ἀχυρώδης</term> ſurfureus. Ariſt. in problem. <term>τί ἀχυρωδέστατον τοῦ αἰγείρου δακρύου</term>. quantum in farina est ſurfurum, maximè, deuritur. Nihil ſurfurei in arbuti fructu. Corrigut. <term>κεφαλώδης</term>. Pomum, inquiunt, arbuti non levem habet exteriorem cutem, ut ceraſum aut prunum, ſed multis minutis corpusculis extantibus aſperum, ut fraga, hoc Græci <term>κεφαλώδες</term> vocant. Non loquitur de facie ac forma Dioſcorides, ſed de ſapore. <term>ἰδιόδωρον</term> ἀχυρώδης, inquit, (rectiùs alii <term>ἀχυλώδη</term> legunt, ) ſic enim ſcribendum, non <term>κακεχώδης, ἀχυλώδες</term> in neutro genere. Ad <term>καρπὸν</term> referri voces hę debent, guſtu eſt ſubauſterus, alioquin inſipidus. Non ineptè fortaſſe quis reſtitueret ἢ <term>ἐρυθρὸν, ἀχυρώδη, ἰδιόδωρον ἢ κακοστόμαχον καὶ κεφαλαλγῆ</term>. ut vox <term>ἀχυρώδη</term> de forma intelligatur, non ſapore. Multis enim particulis quaſi ſurfureis ac paleaceis conſtat, Plinius. Aliud corpus terrestribus fragis, aliud congeneri earum unedoni: quod ſolum pomum ſimile fructū terræ gignit. Non incidit Plinio, adrachnes fructus, quem inimæculo ſimilem docet Theophraſtus, fructui quoque terræ, id est, frago ſimilem eſſe. Ad fragi arbutique ſimilitudinem, quam habent, reſpexit poeta Sulmonenſis, cum ait. Arbuteos fœtus montanaq; fraga legebant. Sunt qui fraga montana arbuti fructum exiſtimant, cum ab arbuto particulâ, que, diſtungat poeta. Fortaſſe non malè quis apud Plinium leget. Quod ſolum pomum ſimile fructui terræ; gignitur; quomodo in antiquiſſimo noſtro Veneto codice legitur, Fructū & Arborum fructus, in alto non humi gignuntur, ut herbarum, quarum fructus in terra ſuſi, ideo **terræ & frutici ſimile pomū** gignis dicit. Fraga & unedones. <term>ἰσχύας κρεμᾶς ἀπὸ τ’ ἀνδράχνην</term> Græci ſeparant. Peſſimè gloſſarū auctor fraga <term>μιμαίκυλα</term>. Nec melius Apuleius, Comarū Græci Romani fragum nuncupant, naſcitur locis opacis, & mundis & collibus. Nemo, cui mens ſana, <term>κόμαρον</term> fragum dixit; frago comparat arbuti fructum Plinius, & cum eo optimè comparari poteſt; ſed fragum à Græcis <term>κόμαρον</term> vocari, non tradit. Arbor est <term>κόμαρος</term>: humillima herba fragum. Arbuti fructus è tenuibus dependent pediculis; fragis ſimiles, orbiculati, multò majores, & rotundis prunis interdum magnitudine pares, multis minuſculis corpuſculis paleaceis conſtantes, initio virides, deinde flaveſcentes, maturi elegantiſſimo rubro colore conſpicui, (ut non immeritò Poeta Ovid. cecinerit. — Pomoque onerata rubenti. Arbutus —) interiore tamen carne palleſcentes, nullo intus officulo, ſed exiguis tantummodo ſeminibus, milio non majoribus, tenui mēbrana in meditullio obductis, edules, gustu ſubauſtero, alioquin inſipido, à tenuis fortunæ hominibus expetiti, uti, & à turdis, & merulis, qui his per hyemem veſcuntur. hyeme enim maturi eſſe ſolent, ut ſcribit Virgilius.

> Venit Hyems, teritur Sicyonia bacca trapetis,
> Glande ſues læti redeunt, dant arbuta ſylvæ.
> Frons hædis expetitur, ut idem ait.
> Dulce satis humor, depulſis arbutus hædis.

### Hactenus de arbuto.

<term>Παιδέρωτος ἢ τὸ φῦλλον καὶ ἡ ἀνδράχνη</term>. Supra lib. I. ex auctoritate Plinii dixi ſcribendum <term>ἀδράχνη</term>. qui lib. 13. cap. 22. hæc tradit; Adrachnen omnes ſerè Græci portulacæ nomine interpretantur, cum ſit herba & andrachne vocetur, unius litteræ diverſitate. Doctiſſimus, & in litteris facilè princeps, legit Andrachnen omnes ſerè Græculi ſed quid eſt, inquit, quod ait Plinius andrachnen arborem ab andrachne herba quæ portulaca eſt, unius litteræ diverſitate diſcerni? Eruditi viri adrachnen ſcribendum ajunt, quum arborem paſsim indigetant : poſtea nulla diverſitas litteræ inter andrachnen & adrachnen, ſed una littera minus est quã in altera dictione. Libri hoc loco ſcriptū habent andraden omnind pro andraclen, nam ita in ſequentib. planè præferunt. Ceterùm andracle est ſilvestris arbor, neque in plantis naſcens, ſimilis unedoni, folio tantum minore: Ita enim ſcribitur in antiquis exemplarib. Et paulò poſt : Similis & apharce bifera æque quã andracle, ſed & lib. 16. c. 22. Ita diſertim in optimo Thuanaon inveni, inter utraque genera ſunt andracile, in Græcia & ubique unedo. quod certum pro andracile, pro andracle vel andrachle. Hæc igitur Plinii ſententia est, <term>ἀνδράχλης</term> dici de arbore, <term>ἀνδράχνης</term> de herba portulaca, literæ unius diverſitate. Sed haud ſcit, vir in omni ſtudiorum genere exercitatiſſimus, an ita diſtincta hæc nomina repererit in exemplaribus Theophraſti, quæ tum extabant. Hodie quæ extant, hanc differentiam non agnoſcunt, ſed <term>ἀνδράχλην</term> utramque vocant, tam arborem quam herbam.

<header>OF THEOPHRASTUS</header>

Theophrastus also observed this in book 1, chapter 15. Theophrastus, when he writes that it blooms in the month of <term>Pyanepsion</term>, means, I believe, that it blooms quite late, even then, when the leaves of other trees are falling. Or, the meaning could be that it then brings forth new flowers again, when the leaves are accustomed to falling, and by that, he demonstrates that it is always seen laden with flowers. But I would not dare to affirm this. He describes the flower very elegantly and accurately; he says <term>λειὸν μὲν</term> <gloss>smooth</gloss>, <term>κρεμαδρῶς</term>. Budæus, as the most learned Constantinus also advises, reads <term>κρεμάδρας</term>. <term>Κρεμάδρα</term> is a vessel destined for keeping leftovers of food, which one might rightly call a hanging repository. The scholiast <term>τοῦτο τὸ σκεῦος εἰς ὁ τὰ σιτίδια ὄψα ἑκάστοτε ἀποτίθεασι, διὰ τὸ μετέωρον εἶναι καὶ κρεμάμενον. κρέμαστρα κρεμάθρα</term> <gloss>this vessel into which they put leftovers and dishes each time, because it is elevated and hanging. A hanger or basket</gloss>. Astronomical and geometrical instruments are hanging, as the interpreter of Aristophanes teaches regarding that passage in the *Clouds*. But in Theophrastus, as the most learned Constantinus advises, it signifies the multifid pedicle by which the fruits are attached; the flowers on the ends of the branches, with a singular appendage, adhere in clusters, white, on one side facing the sun, somewhat reddish, concave, very similar to the flowers of the lily of the valley. These are small, round, gaping, and at the edges denticulated and reflexed.

<margin>Doric Carnius.</margin>
They translate it as either Doric Carnius; I do not know what a Doric Carnius is. Suidas writes that it is a certain festival. <term>Κήρειος ἀπόλλων, κήρνια ἀπόλλωνος ἑορτὴ ἐν Λακεδαιμονίοις</term> <gloss>Cereian Apollo, the festival of the Cereia of Apollo among the Lacedaemonians</gloss>. This has nothing to do with the arbutus. Write <term>κεράνιον δοκανὸν</term>, a Doric capital, or <term>κιονόκρανον</term>, or <term>κεράνιον τοῦ Δωρικοῦ κίονος</term>, the summit or head of a Doric column. Vitruvius calls it the epistyle and capital; according to Pollux, <term>κιονόκρανα, καὶ κεφαλαὶ τῶν κίονων</term> <gloss>column capitals, and heads of columns</gloss>. The deciduous flower can not ineptly be compared to the capital of a column.

<term>Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς</term> <gloss>The fruit</gloss>. Pliny rendered these things in this sense. The fruit ripens in a year and blooms at the same time, growing underneath, and the previous one is gathered (I read from an ancient codex *coquitur* [is cooked], that is, it matures, as botanists speak). Whether it is male or a sterile female, the authors do not agree. I am surprised Theophrastus did not delineate the fruit. Dioscorides reports these things about it: <term>καρπὸς ἔχων ὡς κηκυμήλου μέγεθος, ἀπύρηνον μιμαίκυλον</term> (thus it should be read, as we taught above) <term>κιχλίδιον, πεπανοῦθαι δὲ ὑπόκιρρον ἢ ἐρυθρὸν, ἰδιόδωρον ἀχυρώδης, κακοστόμαχον καὶ κεφαλαλγῆ</term>. (Write <term>ἀχυρώδη</term>, if this word is not also corrupted, and <term>κεφαλαλγῆ</term>: for these words must be referred to the <term>κομάρου καρπόν</term>, that is, the arbutus fruit.) Bringing forth fruit the size of a plum, without a stone, which is nicknamed <term>mimaikylon</term>, and which, when it matures, appears yellowish or reddish, in eating it is bran-like/chaffy, it is adverse to the stomach and excites a headache. The word <term>ἀχυρώδης</term> means bran-like. Aristotle in his *Problems* asks: <term>τί ἀχυρωδέστατον τοῦ αἰγείρου δακρύου</term> <gloss>what is most chaff-like of the poplar's tear?</gloss> As much chaff as there is in flour, mostly, it is burnt. There is nothing chaff-like in the arbutus fruit. Correct to <term>κεφαλώδες</term>. The fruit, they say, does not have a smooth outer skin like a cherry or plum, but is rough with many small, protruding particles, like a strawberry; the Greeks call this <term>κεφαλώδες</term> <gloss>head-like</gloss>. Dioscorides is not speaking of the appearance and form, but of the taste. <term>ἰδιόδωρον</term> <gloss>peculiar/distinctive</gloss>, <term>ἀχυρώδες</term>, he says (others more correctly read <term>ἀχυλώδη</term>), for so it should be written, not <term>κακεχώδης, ἀχυλώδες</term> in the neuter gender. These words should be referred to <term>καρπὸν</term> <gloss>fruit</gloss>; in taste, it is slightly austere, otherwise insipid. One might perhaps not ineptly restore <term>ἢ ἐρυθρὸν, ἀχυρώδη, ἰδιόδωρον ἢ κακοστόμαχον καὶ κεφαλαλγῆ</term> so that the word <term>ἀχυρώδη</term> is understood of the form, not the taste. For it consists of many particles, as it were bran-like and chaffy, says Pliny. One thing is the body of terrestrial strawberries, another of their congener the *unedo*; which is the only fruit that produces a fruit of the earth. It did not occur to Pliny that the fruit of the *adrachne*, which Theophrastus teaches is similar to the *mimaikylon*, is also similar to the fruit of the earth, that is, the strawberry. The Sulmonensian poet [Ovid] looked to the similarity of the strawberry and the arbutus when he said: *They gathered arbute fruits and mountain strawberries.* There are those who think mountain strawberries are the fruit of the arbutus, whereas the poet distinguishes them by a particle. Perhaps one would not be wrong to read in Pliny: *Which is the only fruit similar to the fruit of the earth;* as it is read in our most ancient Venetian codex. He says that the fruit of trees is not produced in the high places, not on the ground like herbs, the fruits of which are scattered on the earth, therefore he says it produces a **fruit similar to the earth and the shrub**. Strawberries and *unedones*. The Greeks separate <term>ἰσχύας κρεμᾶς ἀπὸ τ’ ἀνδράχνην</term>. The author of the glossaries very poorly calls strawberries <term>μιμαίκυλα</term>. Nor is Apuleius any better: *The Greeks and Romans call the Arbutus a strawberry, it is born in shady places, and in clean places and hills.* No one with a sound mind has called <term>κόμαρον</term> a strawberry; Pliny compares the arbutus fruit to a strawberry, and it can be compared with it very well; but he does not report that the strawberry is called <term>κόμαρον</term> by the Greeks. The tree is <term>κόμαρος</term>; the very low herb is the strawberry. The fruit of the arbutus hangs from thin pedicles; they are similar to strawberries, round, much larger, and sometimes equal in size to round plums, consisting of many tiny chaffy particles, at first green, then turning yellow, and when mature they are distinguished by a most elegant red color (so that the poet Ovid not undeservedly sang: *—And the arbutus laden with reddening fruit—*) yet they are pale in their inner flesh, with no pit inside, but only tiny seeds, no larger than millet, covered with a thin membrane in the middle, edible, in taste slightly austere, otherwise insipid, sought after by people of meager means, as well as by thrushes and blackbirds, which eat them during the winter. For they are accustomed to be mature in the winter, as Virgil writes:

> Winter comes, the Sicyonian berry is ground in the mills,
> Joyful, the pigs return with the acorn, the woods give arbutus.
> The foliage is sought by the goats, as he also says.
> Sweet moisture for the sated, the arbutus for the weaned goats.

### Thus far concerning the arbutus.

<term>Παιδέρωτος ἢ τὸ φῦλλον καὶ ἡ ἀνδράχνη</term>. Above, in book 1, on the authority of Pliny, I said that <term>ἀδράχνη</term> should be written, who in book 13, chapter 22, reports these things: *Almost all the Greeks interpret the Adrachne by the name of purslane, although it is an herb and is called andrachne, with a diversity of one letter.* The most learned man, and easily the prince of letters, reads *Andrachnen* [as] almost all the Greeks; but what is it, he says, that Pliny says that the *andrachne* tree is distinguished from the *andrachne* herb, which is purslane, by the diversity of one letter? Learned men say that *adrachne* should be written when they signify the tree: then there is no diversity of a letter between *andrachnen* and *adrachnen*, but there is one letter less than in the other word. The books in this place have written *andraden* entirely instead of *andraclen*, for so in what follows they clearly prefer it. Moreover, the *andracle* is a wild tree, not growing among plants, similar to the *unedo*, with only a smaller leaf: for so it is written in ancient exemplars. And a little later: *Similar also is the biferal apharce, equally with the andracle, but also in book 16, ch. 22.* I found this distinctly in the best Thuanian [manuscript], among both kinds there is the *andracile*, in Greece and everywhere the *unedo*. Which is certain for *andracile*, for *andracle* or *andrachle*. This, therefore, is the opinion of Pliny, that <term>ἀνδράχλης</term> is said of the tree, <term>ἀνδράχνης</term> of the herb purslane, by the diversity of one letter. But the man, most exercised in every kind of study, does not know if he found these names so distinguished in the exemplars of Theophrastus that were then extant. Those that exist today do not recognize this difference, but call both <term>ἀνδράχλην</term>, both the tree and the...

<header>SERVIUS</header>

...as shortly after <note>262</note> "he gives to the man to have." But this is granted to poets.
MAGNVM TALENTVM as we said <note>112</note> a certain small [thing], but he called it 'great' by comparison with another.

250. CIRCVM that is, in the outer part.

251. MAEANDRO DVPLICI winding. And he says this: on the cloak was a winding purple [border] capable of turning back on itself, in the manner of the Maeander, a river of the province of Caria, which is very winding. MELIBOEA others think Milesian. Instead of Meliboean: now Meliboea is a city of Thessaly.

252. REGIVS of Troy, the son of the king of Phrygia.

253. FATIGAT the praise of the depiction, as if he were carrying [it].

254. ACER that is, swift. PRAEPES here means flying.

255. SVBLIMEM on high.

256. PALMAS AD SIDERA TENDVNT either wondering, or rebuking the gods.

258. VIRTUTE SECVNDVM because he had won by the favor of the gods: whence also worthy prizes are given: to him a cloak, containing the story of the gods, to this [man] a breastplate, that is, the emblem of virtue.

259. HAMIS AVROQVE with golden hooks.

261. SIMOENTA comes from the Greek nominative, ending not in <term>is</term>, but in <term>eis</term>. SVB ILIO ALTO the 'o' becomes short with the following vowel.

262. DECVS ET TVTAMEN because [it is] triple and golden.

263. PHEGEVS SAGARISQVE by speaking by name he added praise.

4. ULPIANUS lib. 15. ad Edictum.
Et, si pauciores fuerint nati, residuum ei (1) pro rata aderescere : si plures, quam tres : decrescere de ea parte, ex qua heres factus est.

*De institutione posthumorum et extranei.*

5. PAULUS lib. 17. ad Edictum.
Illud sciendum est, si mulier prægnans non sit, existimetur autem prægnans esse, interim filium heredem esse ex asse (2), quanquam ignoret (3) se ex asse heredem esse.
§. 1. Idem est in extraneo, si ex certa portione heres institutus sit : ex reliqua, posthumi. † Quod si forte ita institutio facta est, quolcumque mihi nati erunt, et Lucius Titius pro virilibus portionibus heredes mihi sunto : habebit hæsitationem, numquid adire non possit, atque qui in testamento portionem suam nescit? Sed utilius est, posse eum adire, qui (4) nescit portionem, si cætera, quæ oportet eum scire, non ignoret.

*De portione petitori conferenda. 1. De sumptibus.*

6. ULPIANUS lib. 6. Opinionum.
Sorori (5), quam coheredem fratribus quatuor in bonis matris esse placuit, quinta portio, pro portionibus, quæ ad eos pertinuit, cedet (6) : ita ut singuli in quarta, quam antehac habere credebantur, non amplius ei quintam conferant.
§. 1. Sumptus, qui propter onera totius hereditatis justi fiunt, ei, qui patroni (7) jure portionem (8) evicerit, pro rata computentur.

*Quid consequimur hoc judicio.*

7. JULIANUS lib. 8. Digestorum.
Non (9) possumus consequi per hereditatis petitionem id, quod familiæ herciscundæ judicio consequimur, ut a communione discedamus (10) : cum ad officium Judicis (11) nihil amplius pertineat, quam ut partem (12) hereditatis pro indiviso restitui mihi jubeat.

*Si possessor partem defendat, pro parte cedat.*

8. IDEM lib. 48. Digestorum.
Permittendum erit possessori hereditatis, partem (13) quidem hereditatis defendere (14), parte vero cedere. Nec enim prohibet, aliquem totam hereditatem possidere, et partem scire dimidiam ad se pertinere, de altera parte controversiam non facere.

*De procuratore, et herede heredis ante testatorem defuncti.*

9. PAULUS lib. 3. Epitomarum Alfeni Digestorum.
Cum multi heredes instituti essent, ex his unus in Asia erat, ejus procurator venditionem fecit, et pecuniam pro parte ejus abstulerat : postea apparuerit, cum, qui in Asia erat, antea decessisse, instituto ex parte dimidia herede procuratore suo, et ex parte, alio : Quæsitum est, quemadmodum pecunia ex hereditate petenda esset? Responsum est, ab eo, qui procurator (15) ejus fuisset, totam hereditatem, quia ex hereditate ea pecunia fuisset, quæ ad procuratorem ex venditione pervenisset, petere eos oportere : et nihilominus partem dimidiam hereditatis a coheredibus ejus. ita fore, sive omnis ea pecunia penes eum, qui procurator fuisset, resideret, ut omnem per Judicem ab eodem recuperarent : sive is partem dimidiam coheredi suo reddidisset, ipsum ex dimidia parte, [et] ex dimidia coheredes ejus condemnarent.

<column-break/>

*De eo, qui negotia hereditaria nomine absentis gessit.*

10. PAPINIANUS lib. 6. Quæstionum.
Cum heredis ex parte instituti filius, qui patrem suum ignorabat vivo testatore decessisse, partem hereditatis, nomine patris, [ut] absentis , administraverit (16), et pecunias, distractis rebus, acceperit, hereditas ab eo peti non potest (17) : quia neque (18) pro herede, neque pro possessore pretia possidet, sed ut filius patris negotium curavit : Negotiorum autem gestorum actio cæteris coheredibus, ad quos portio defuncti pertinet, dabitur. Illud [enim] utique non est metuendum, ne etiam patris (a quo forte exheredatus est) teneatur heredibus, quasi negotia hereditaria gesserit : cum id, quod administravit, non fuerit paternæ hereditatis. Nam et si negotiorum gestorum actio sit ei, cujus nomine per-ceptum est : ei cujus nomine, restitui æquum est. Sed in proposito neque patris negotia fuerunt, qui esse desierat : neque paternæ successionis, quæ fuerunt alterius hereditatis. Quod si filius iste patri suo heres extitit, et movet controversiam, quod pater ejus, postquam heres extitit, mortem obierit, ille tractatus incurrit, an ipse sibi causam (19) possessionis mutare videatur? Quoniam tamen qui negotia hereditaria gessit, et debitor esse cœpit, postea faciens controversiam hereditatis, ut juris possessor, convenitur, idem etiam in hoc filio respondendum erit.

4. ULPIANUS, book 15 on the Edict.
And, if fewer are born, the remainder accrues to him <note>original: "ei"</note> in proportion: if more than three, it decreases from that share from which he was made heir.

Concerning the institution of posthumous heirs and an outsider.

5. PAULUS, book 17 on the Edict.
That must be known: if a woman is not pregnant, but is thought to be pregnant, in the meantime the son is heir to the whole, although he is ignorant that he is heir to the whole.
§ 1. The same applies to an outsider, if he has been instituted heir for a certain portion: for the remainder, posthumous children. But if by chance the institution was made thus: "Whosoever shall be born to me, and Lucius Titius, shall be my heirs for their proportional shares": it will have a hesitation, whether he who does not know his portion in the testament can enter upon the inheritance? But it is more useful that he who does not know his portion can enter, if he is not ignorant of the other things which he ought to know.

Concerning the portion to be conferred upon the petitioner. 1. Concerning expenses.

6. ULPIANUS, book 6 of Opinions.
To the sister, whom it was decided should be a co-heir to the four brothers in the mother's property, a fifth portion shall yield, for the portions that pertained to them: in such a way that each of them, in the fourth which they were previously believed to have, do not confer more than a fifth upon her.
§ 1. Expenses which are made justly on account of the burdens of the whole inheritance shall be computed in proportion for him who has recovered a portion by the right of a patron.

What we obtain by this action.

7. JULIANUS, book 8 of the Digests.
We cannot obtain through the petition for an inheritance that which we obtain by the action for the partition of an inheritance, that we may depart from the communion: since nothing more pertains to the office of the judge than that he orders the part of the inheritance to be restored to me in an undivided state.

If a possessor defends a part, he may yield for a part.

8. THE SAME, book 48 of the Digests.
It shall be permitted to the possessor of an inheritance to defend a part of the inheritance, while yielding on another part. For it does not prohibit someone from possessing the whole inheritance, and knowing that a half-share pertains to himself, while not making a controversy regarding the other part.

Concerning a procurator, and the heir of an heir who died before the testator.

9. PAULUS, book 3 of the Epitomes of Alfenus' Digests.
When many heirs had been instituted, one of them was in Asia; his procurator made a sale and had taken the money for his share: afterwards it appeared that he who was in Asia had died beforehand, with his procurator instituted as heir for a half-share, and another for the other half: It was asked, in what manner the money from the inheritance ought to be petitioned? It was answered that they ought to petition the whole inheritance from him who had been his procurator, because that money had come from the inheritance which reached the procurator from the sale: and nevertheless petition for the half-share of the inheritance from his co-heirs. Thus it will be, whether all that money resided with him who had been the procurator, so that they recovered everything from the same person through a judge: or whether he had returned the half-share to his co-heir, they would condemn him for the half-share, and his co-heirs for the half.

<column-break/>

Concerning him who managed hereditary business in the name of an absent person.

10. PAPINIANUS, book 6 of Questions.
When the son of an heir instituted for a part, who was ignorant that his father had died while the testator was alive, administered a part of the inheritance in the name of his father, as if he were absent, and received monies, having sold the things, the inheritance cannot be petitioned from him: because he possesses the prices neither as an heir nor as a possessor, but managed the business as the son of his father: However, an action for managed business <note>original: "negotiorum gestorum"</note> will be given to the other co-heirs to whom the portion of the deceased pertains. That, indeed, is certainly not to be feared, that he might also be held liable to the heirs of the father (by whom perhaps he was disinherited), as if he had managed hereditary business: since that which he administered was not part of the father's inheritance. For even if an action for managed business exists for him in whose name it was received, it is equitable that it be restored to him in whose name it was. But in the case proposed, it was neither the business of the father, who had ceased to exist, nor of the father's succession, which belonged to another inheritance. But if this son became heir to his father, and moves a controversy, because his father died after he became heir, that discussion occurs: whether he seems to change the cause of possession for himself? Since, however, he who managed hereditary business and began to be a debtor is afterwards sued when he makes a controversy about the inheritance as a possessor of right, the same must be answered regarding this son.

Peter knelt down, leaned toward his son, and embraced his head.
— Nothing, nothing, my dear! — the Tsarevich whispered. — I am fine, everything is fine. Let the Lord’s will be done in everything.
The father pressed his lips to his son’s lips. But he had already weakened and slumped in his arms; his eyes clouded over, his gaze faded.
Peter stood up, swaying.
— Will he die? — he asked the court physician.
— Perhaps, he will survive until night, — the latter answered.
Everyone ran to the Tsar and led him out of the chamber.
Peter suddenly became completely collapsed, weakened, subdued, and became obedient as a child: he went where he was led, did what he was told.
In the vestibule of the torture chamber, Tolstoy, noticing that the Tsar’s hands were covered in blood, ordered a washbasin to be brought. He began to wash obediently. The water turned pink.
They led him out of the fortress, seated him in a boat, and took him to the palace.
Tolstoy and Menshikov did not leave the Tsar's side. To occupy and distract him, they spoke of extraneous matters. He listened calmly, answered reasonably. He gave resolutions, signed papers. But later he could not remember what he had done then, as if he had spent all that time in a dream or in a faint. He did not bring up the subject of his son himself, as if he had forgotten about him entirely.
Finally, in the fifth hour of the evening, when they reported to Tolstoy and Menshikov that the Tsarevich was dying, they had to remind him about his son. He listened distractedly, as if he did not understand what they were talking about. Nevertheless, he sat in the boat again and went to the fortress.
The Tsarevich had been moved from the torture chamber to the casemate in his former place. He had not regained consciousness.

Acilius, however, the man who wrote a history in Greek, says that there were more who returned to the camp with the same fraud, in order to be freed from their oath, and that they were marked by the censors with every ignominy. Let this be the end of this topic. For it is clear what is done with a timid, humble, submissive, and broken spirit; such would have been the act of Regulus if he had wanted either to speak about the captives what seemed useful to himself—not what he had judged useful for the Republic—or had wanted to remain at home. Such things are not useful, because they are shameful, foul, and base. There remains the fourth part, which consists of decorum, moderation, modesty, restraint, and temperance. Can anything, therefore, be useful that is contrary to this chorus of such virtues? But the philosophers called Cyrenaics and Annicereans, from Aristippus, placed every good in pleasure, and judged that virtue was to be praised for this reason: that it was the producer of pleasure. With these obsolete, Epicurus flourishes, a helper and author of almost the same opinion. With these, one must struggle with all one's might—as the saying goes—if one is determined to protect and keep honor. For if not only utility, but all happy life, is contained in a firm constitution of the body and the explored hope of that constitution (as was written by Metrodorus), certainly this utility—and indeed the greatest utility (for so they judge)—will fight with honor. For where will the first place be given to prudence? Will it be to seek out pleasures from everywhere? How miserable is the servitude of virtue serving pleasure. What, moreover, is the office of prudence? Is it to select pleasures? Suppose there is nothing more pleasant than that; what can be imagined that is more base? Now, he who

It is also faulty to assume as an argument that which is the subject of the investigation: as if someone, arguing a case of theft, says he is a wicked, greedy, and fraudulent man: that his having stolen from him is proof of that fact. It is also faulty to dissolve a controversy with a controversy, in this way: "It is not appropriate for the Censors to satisfy you regarding this matter, on the grounds that he says he could not be present as he had sworn: for if he had not come to the army, would he say this to the Military Tribune?" This is faulty because the matter is not settled or adjudicated, but rather hindered and placed in a similar controversy used as an example. It is also faulty when that about which the main controversy exists is barely explained, and it is left as if it had been resolved, in this way:
The statement speaks openly, if you understand:
He orders arms to be given to one such as the one who wore them was,
If we are eager to master Pergamum:
Which I profess to be my own. For it is right that I enjoy
My brother's arms, and that they be adjudicated to me,
Whether because I am a kinsman, or because I am a rival in virtue.

It is also faulty for the speaker to dissent from himself in his own speech, and to say the opposite of what he had said before, in this way:
What reason I should accuse him for, I cannot unravel by searching.
For if he is feared, why accuse him, who is upright?
But if he possesses a shameless disposition of mind,
Why accuse him, who considers that of little account in hearing?
He seems to have shown in no inconvenient way why he should not accuse. What, then, does he say afterward?

You would scarcely believe, Callistus, how much I have been soothed by your entire speech. Already I seem almost to discern those <term>species</term> <gloss>forms or archetypes</gloss> of the Platonists. But I would like you to respond somewhat more distinctly to the Aristotelian arguments, so that I may more confidently mock those who boast that the books of the ancient philosophers can be understood by no mortals, except by those who have spent all their time entirely without any knowledge of either language <note>referring to Greek and Latin</note>, either in those contentious schools of theirs, or reading books filled with every filth and barbarism.

CAL. Have you not read, Polycarpus, what your Cicero feels and says about this type of man?

POLY. I have read, both elsewhere and in the <term>Tusculan Disputations</term>, that there are some who read their own books only with their own followers, and wish for the same license of writing to be granted to themselves if there are any others.

CAL. I do not mean this, Polycarpus.

POLY. What then, I ask you?

CAL. In the books <term>On Divination</term>, what I am saying is written, if I am not mistaken.

POLY. What, pray tell?

CAL. It is a discussion about Democritus, I believe.

POLY. Now I remember, Callistus. Indeed, that among the <term>Physici</term> <gloss>natural philosophers</gloss>, there is no breed of men more arrogant.

CAL. That is the very thing. However, to gratify you as you demand honest things, I will now endeavor to recount to you those matters which, as I was saying a moment ago, I did not discover myself, but committed to memory after reading them in the books of the Platonists. Nevertheless, if in turn [you grant] me...

If the wealthy Gallita, and Paccius, the childless one, has begun
To be ill, the whole portico is legitimately covered with
Fixed tablets; there exist those who promise a hecatomb.
Inasmuch as here there are no elephants for sale,
Nor in Latium, nor anywhere under our sky is such
A beast conceived, but sought from a swarthy race
And reddened trees, and fed on the field of Turnus,
The herd of Caesar, prepared to serve no
Private individual, inasmuch as they were wont to serve the Tyrian

Their ancestors, and to carry on their backs the cohorts,
Some part of the war, and the troop going into battle.

And falls as a sacred victim before the Lares,
Worthy of such great gods, and of their legacy-hunters.
For the other, if you permit it, will vow to slaughter
From his herd of slaves the great and most beautiful bodies
Of each, or he will impose ribbons on his boys and the foreheads
Of his handmaids; and if any Iphigenia is nubile
To him at home, he will give her to the altars, even if
He does not hope for the secret substitute of the tragic deer.
I praise my fellow citizen, nor do I compare a thousand ships
To his will; for if the sick man escapes Libitina <note>the goddess of funerals</note>,
He will erase the tablets, enclosed in the trap of the net,
After a merit, indeed, to be wondered at, and perhaps he will
Briefly give everything to Pacuvius alone; he, proud,
Will walk with his rivals defeated. Therefore, you see what
Great reward for his work the slaughtered Mycenean girl makes.
May Pacuvius live, I pray, or possess all of Nestor,
May he possess as much as Nero plundered, may he match
Gold with mountains, nor love anyone, nor be loved by anyone.

He indicates the decorum of the saints by a similitude, and it is a very evident argument: for as stars cannot but shine, so the pious ought always to declare their duty by good works. A "crooked generation" here is the world, that is, the assembly of wicked men, and they have the nature of night. The pious living among them are stars, showing the way to the heavens by shining. ### Der Vulkan auf der Insel Tanna. *)

Den 4ten August 1774 erblickte Cook, da er sich der Insel Tanna näherte, ein großes Feuer. Den Morgen darauf fand er, daß der feurige Schein, welchen er in der Nacht gesehen hatte, von einem Vulkane verursacht wurde, der mit einem starken, und in einer weiten Entfernung hörbaren Geräusche, eine große Menge Feuer und Rauch von sich gab. Diese ganze Nacht hindurch sowohl, als den 11ten, war der Berg sehr unruhig. Er machte ein furchtbares Getöse und es stieg bey jeder Explosion desselben eine ungeheure Säule von Feuer und Rauch aus seinem Krater empor. Die Ausbrüche erfolgten alle 3 oder 4 Minuten, wobey der Vulkan zugleich große Steine hoch in die Luft schleuderte. Herr Forster ging mit seiner Gesellschaft auf den Hügel an der westlichen Seite des Hafens, wo sie drey Stellen fanden, aus welchen durch die Ritzen oder Spalten in der Erde ein Rauch von schwefelichem Geruche hervordrang. Der Boden umher war außerordentlich heiß und glimmte oder brannte.

### The volcano on the island of Tanna. <note>original: *) James Cook's Voyage towards the south Pole, and round the world, in the years 1772, 1773, 1774 and 1775. Vol. II. 4th edition. London, 1784. 4to. With copperplate engravings.</note>

On August 4, 1774, as Cook approached the island of Tanna, he sighted a great fire. The following morning, he found that the fiery glow he had seen in the night was caused by a volcano, which, with a powerful noise audible at a great distance, emitted a large quantity of fire and smoke. Throughout this whole night, as well as on the 11th, the mountain was very restless. It made a terrible rumbling, and at each explosion, an enormous pillar of fire and smoke rose from its crater. The eruptions occurred every 3 or 4 minutes, during which the volcano simultaneously hurled large rocks high into the air. Mr. Forster went with his company to the hill on the western side of the harbor, where they found three places from which a smoke with a sulfuric odor emerged through cracks or fissures in the earth. The ground all around was extraordinarily hot and was smoldering or burning.

When Metrodorus had given himself entirely to the new doctrine, in which he saw all salvation included, he did not hesitate to follow the heads of the discipline to their final limits. Thus it happens that the things which he emitted from an elevated mind, full of a single study, and pronounced with the greatest force of expression, appear impudent and humble.

But I shall now make an end to the preface. What else must be said about the character and opinions of Metrodorus, I prefer to note against the individual writings and fragments. In what I have set forth here, I have primarily aimed to refute the opinions of Hirzel. I will have to recur to him quite often, for I think the whole chapter of his otherwise excellent book, which deals with the disagreements of the Epicureans, rests on the weakest foundations.

# and the six blameworthy morals of the old

they also fail. Fearing therefore to suffer defect, they are illiberal. Again, they are illiberal because of the experience of time. Because, since they have lived for many years, it is credible that they have suffered many needs. Fearing therefore to suffer need, they are illiberal. It happens also that they are illiberal because they live more by memory than by hope. For they think of having lived much in the past and being about to live little in the future. And because memory is of past things and hope is of future things, therefore they do not live by hope, nor do they confide in those things which they ought to acquire in the future, but they live by memory, confiding in those things which they have acquired in the past. Therefore they are illiberal, not distributing easily what has been acquired. Fifth, they are of bad hope. For they hope for nothing good, but believe themselves to fail in everything. For hope is of future things, memory of past things. Since, therefore, the old have lived much in the past and believe themselves about to live little in the future, therefore they fail in hoping and think they will do little things. For they do not live and delight in hoping, but rather in remembering; therefore they are of difficult hope. Sixth, they are shameless and unblushing. For because the old are illiberal, they care more about the vile than about the honest. And thus they study more those things which import utility than those things which require the state of honor. Therefore, since modesty is the fear of dishonor, it does not apply to the old because they themselves care more about utility than about honor. Whence, the reason why someone is modest, as the philosopher says, is this: because he seeks to be had in honor and to be reputed honest. But the old, just as they fail in life and in humors and in natural heat, so they fail in spirit, not caring about how they are reputed; wherefore it happens that they are shameless. One cause could also be assigned, which is common to all things touched upon. For the old are cold. For it belongs to the cold to constipate and constrain; therefore, the old, from coldness, are constipated and retracted in themselves and rendered as if immobile, so that they dare nothing, believe nothing, hope for nothing, do not care to excel nor to be reputed. <note>A marginal mark resembles a hand or flourish.</note> Having elicited the morals of the young and the old, both praiseworthy and detestable, the morals of those who are in the [intermediate] state are easily patent. For they are in a state that mediates between the old and the young. Whatever of praiseworthiness is found in the young or in the old can be in those who are in the state. For they are not too hot as the young, nor too cold as the old; they hold the mean between both. Therefore, they are timid where one ought to fear, and bold where one ought to be bold. Similarly, because they are not inexperienced in everything as the young, nor deceived in everything as the old, therefore they do not believe everything as the young do because of inexperience, nor do they disbelieve entirely as the old do, in that the old are deceived in many things; but they behave in a middle way. Therefore, in the second [book] of the Rhetoric, it is said that those who are in the state are not believing everything nor disbelieving everything, but judge more according to truth. Furthermore, they are not impatient as the young, nor fearful and useless as the old. But as it is said in the second [book] of the Rhetoric, they are manly in temperance and tempered in manliness. Universally, I shall say that whatever of praiseworthiness is found in the old or in the young can be found in those who are in the state. And whatever of blameworthiness is found in the old or in the young can be excluded by those who are in the state. Thus, therefore, one must speak about the morals of men. Not, however, that these things have necessity, because the old can be liberal and magnanimous, and the young can also be tempered and stable. But these things are to be understood according to a certain propensity and inclination that is according to the natural course and order. Therefore, it follows that the master ought to be an orderer. Whence the master consists in equating. It is said that he who departs more from reality departs through an abundance of reason. But if those things which are [should be] are denied and the lower things are confirmed...

And even these failed attempts are not always a proof of a lack of power of formation, because even where it is genuine, it often takes a completely false direction by wanting to place before its imagination what belongs before its eye, or before its eye what belongs before its ear.

Just because nature does not always allow the inherent power of formation to reach complete maturity and development, or allows it to take a false path on which it can never develop, genuine beauty remains rare. And because nature also allows the common and the bad to arise unhindered from the pretentious instinct for formation, genuine beauty and nobility distinguish themselves precisely through this, through their rare value, from the bad and the common.

In the capacity for feeling, there thus always remains the gap that is filled only by the result of the power of formation.—The power of formation and the capacity for feeling relate to one another like man and woman. For the power of formation is also, at the first emergence of its work, in the moment of highest enjoyment, simultaneously a capacity for feeling and generates, like nature, the imprint of its essence out of itself.

Both the capacity for feeling and the power of formation are therefore grounded in the finer weave of the organization, insofar as the latter is a complete or at least almost complete imprint of the relations of the great whole of nature in all its points of contact. Now I devote my efforts to settling affairs, so that if our friend, that patron of the fine arts, reaches that highest pinnacle of dignity, we may hasten there as soon as possible. For he has often declared, most lovingly, both in letters and in direct conversation, that he wishes to look after my interests. For me, however, everything depends on being allowed to enjoy literary leisure, with no concern for domestic matters to interrupt. If we achieve this, let ambition thrive; we will live for ourselves and the Muses, and indeed with this spirit, that we attribute everything to God, on whom alone true happiness depends: that this seems the same to you, I easily infer from your letters. I am held by a wonderful desire to come to you: but many things snatch this opportunity away, especially my sick son, who I am firmly convinced is most dear to you, both for the sake of our friendship and for our new connection. If I hear that you have been strengthened after your illness, I will bear these domestic inconveniences with a calmer mind. Therefore, you will grant this to our love, which your virtue brought forth, your kindness nourishes, and increases, that you will also take the most diligent care of your health for our sake. Farewell. Venice.

### I. AD INDICEM TERMINOLOGICUM.

1. Nomina philosophorum per compendia notantur, praeterea alia sigla compendiaque adhibentur, quae pag. 1 collecta sunt.
2. Singulis locis nomen philosophi auctoris additum est; Chrysippi nomen semper fere praetermissum in altero et tertio volumine, ubi nullius nomen adscripsi, subaudiendum est, veluti Z. I 47, 23. III 17, 19 prior locus ad Zenonem, alter ad Chrysippum auctorem referendus est.
3. Ubique numero voluminis omisso proximus numerus antecedens supplendus est.
4. Recepta non sunt vocabula a scriptoribus, qui de doctrina Stoica referunt, ex ipsorum ratione cogitandi usurpata aut a Stoicorum philosophia aliena. Frustra igitur exempli gratia s. v. ἐθνικός, ἁπλῶς πιστός argumentum loci Clementis Alexandrini III frg. 515 hoc in indice quaeres, at ἁπλῶς πιστόν s. v. προκόπτων, ἐθνικόν s. v. φαῦλος invenies.
5. Verba ἅπαξ εἰρημένα ad Stoicorum doctrinam pertinentia ad unum omnia huic indici inserta sunt, praesertim ea, quae in Passowii thesauro verborum non leguntur, velut ἀνεπιזητησία, ἀνταναιρετικός, ἀνυπέραρτος e. c.

### II. AD INDICEM LATINUM.

Vocabula Latina, quibus quod verbum Graecum reddatur, dubitari non potest, in primo indice leguntur; quae res in secundo indice hac nota „=“ designatur; nonnusquam notis „cf.“ vel „vid. s. v.“, qui legunt, ad Graeca verba notione similia relegantur; sed in re dubia ad Latinam vocem numeri tantum paginarum et versuum huius fragmentorum collectionis adscribuntur.
Voces Graecas, quas Romani e sermone Graecorum sumpserunt, velut „dialectica, physica“, in indice Latino omissas esse scias.

### III. AD INDICEM NOMINUM PROPRIORUM.

Hoc indice nomina Stoicorum veterum, praeterea ceterorum philosophorum, deinde eorum scriptorum ac poëtarum, qui a veteribus Stoicis laudantur vel impugnantur, conscribuntur. Cetera nomina sive deorum sive hominum a Stoicis commemorata in primo indice reperies.

### IV. AD INDICEM FONTIUM.

Omnes fere loci ad editiones recentissimas referuntur, etiam quorum scriptorum I. ab Arnim editionibus antiquioribus usus est; veluti Stobaei Florilegii loci non ex Meinekii, sed Hensei editione afferuntur.

# ANNOTATIONS TO THE INDIVIDUAL INDICES.

### I. TO THE TERMINOLOGICAL INDEX.

1. The names of philosophers are indicated by abbreviations, and other symbols and abbreviations are used, which are collected on page 1.
2. In individual places, the name of the authoring philosopher is added; the name of Chrysippus is almost always omitted in the second and third volumes, and where I have not inscribed the name of anyone, it is to be understood, such as Z. I 47, 23. III 17, 19: the former place should be referred to Zeno, the latter to Chrysippus as the author.
3. Everywhere, if the volume number is omitted, the nearest preceding number is to be supplied.
4. Words used by writers who report on Stoic doctrine, taken from their own way of thinking or alien to Stoic philosophy, are not included. You will therefore look in vain in this index, for example, s. v. <term>ethnikos</term> <gloss>national/heathen</gloss>, <term>haplōs pistos</term> <gloss>simply faithful</gloss>, for the argument of the passage of Clement of Alexandria III frg. 515, but you will find <term>haplōs piston</term> <gloss>simply faithful</gloss> s. v. <term>prokoptōn</term> <gloss>one making progress</gloss>, and <term>ethnikon</term> <gloss>national/heathen</gloss> s. v. <term>phaulos</term> <gloss>the base/worthless</gloss>.
5. The words <term>hapax eirēmena</term> <gloss>words occurring only once</gloss> pertaining to Stoic doctrine are all inserted into this index, especially those which are not read in Passow's lexicon, such as <term>anepizētēsia</term> <gloss>unsearchableness</gloss>, <term>antanairetikos</term> <gloss>mutually destructive</gloss>, <term>anyperartos</term> <gloss>unassailable</gloss>, etc.

### II. TO THE LATIN INDEX.

Latin words for which it is not doubtful which Greek word is being rendered are read in the first index; this matter is designated in the second index with the note “=”; sometimes by the notes “cf.” or “vid. s. v.”, those who read are referred to Greek words similar in concept; but in doubtful matters, only the numbers of the pages and lines of this collection of fragments are ascribed to the Latin word.
You should know that Greek words which the Romans took from the language of the Greeks, such as “dialectica, physica”, are omitted in the Latin index.

### III. TO THE INDEX OF PROPER NAMES.

In this index are written the names of the ancient Stoics, as well as those of other philosophers, then those writers and poets who are praised or attacked by the ancient Stoics. You will find other names, whether of gods or men, mentioned by the Stoics, in the first index.

### IV. TO THE INDEX OF SOURCES.

Almost all passages are referred to the most recent editions, even those of writers whose earlier editions were used by I. von Arnim; for instance, the passages from Stobaeus' *Florilegium* are cited not from the edition of Meineke, but from that of Hense.

Therefore, his audacity was chastised by Dorvillius in his <term>Vannus critica</term> <gloss>Critical Winnowing-basket/Sieve</gloss>, Amsterdam 1737, 8vo. This edition was published at Utrecht in 1732, 4to, for in the edition of the previous century, 1753, only the title page of the book was changed. But anyone who has the work of Fischer alone will easily dispense with these editions. He published the poems of Anacreon for the third time in Leipzig, 1793, 8vo, with the annotations of Baxter, Estienne, Faber, and his own, which are very rich in both critical and grammatical content, as well as a most comprehensive variety of readings. See the note on the reading of the Spaletti edition at number 21. Although the very learned old man repeated the poor revision of Baxter, he nevertheless performed a great service for Greek letters through this work of his. For he first added to this third edition the preface of the second edition, in which he discourses most diligently and with no small subtlety of mind on the value of various editions and on those matters which pertain to the literary study of these poems, and inquires whether these poems are rightly attributed to Anacreon. Furthermore, he increased the number of fragments and added epigrams of Greek poets on Anacreon. Compare the preface of Mehlhorn, page VI. The revision of Brunck is entirely new; using the Palatine manuscript <note>original: "Codex Palatinus"</note> copied by Spaletti, and the conjectures of Salmasius, Lennep, and others, he presented a more corrected Anacreon, but also indulging too much in his own wit, he emended many things in passing without providing any reasons. ## *On Orthography.*

Orthography is that which teaches the correct method of writing, from <term>orthos</term> <gloss>correct</gloss>, and <term>graphō</term> <gloss>I write</gloss>.

## *On Accent.*

Accent, <term>prosōdia</term> <gloss>accent/prosody</gloss>, is the rule for pronouncing that which pertains to syllables. For of syllables, some are short, some are long, some are acute, some are grave, some are circumflex, etc.

->The <term>prosōdiai</term> <gloss>accents</gloss> are as follows:<-

<term>makra</term> ¯: the mark of a long (produced) syllable.
<term>bracheia</term> ῠ: the mark of a short syllable.
<term>daseia</term> ʽ: the mark of aspiration, as with the Latins, h.
<term>psilē</term> ʼ: is the mark contrary to aspiration, which the Latins do not have. Commonly it is called the light (tenuous) accent.
<term>oxeia</term> ˊ: the mark of the acute accent.
<term>bareia</term> ˋ: the mark of the grave accent.
<term>perispōmenē</term> ˜: the mark of the circumflex.

S. N. *quilibet, quaelibet, quodlibet* or *quidlibet*, and following that, by adding *libet*.

S. N. *quisquis*, and *quidquid*. A. *quidquid*. A. *a quoquo, a quaqua, a quoquo*; it lacks the other cases.

S. N. *neuter, neutra, neutrum*. G. *neutri, neutrae, neutri*, and *neutrius* among the ancients. D. *neutro, neutrae, neutro*, and the rest like *bonus, bona, bonum*.

*Meus, mea, meum*—of what mode of pronoun is it? The third. Why? Because it is declined through all its cases to the similarity of nouns of the first and second declension, that is, like *bonus, bona, bonum*, except for the vocative *mi*, from the vocative *mee*, where the double and short *e* has been changed into a long *i*, as *o mi pater, o mi fili* <gloss>o my father, o my son</gloss> instead of *mee pater, mee fili*.

There are five pronouns of the third mode: *meus, tuus, suus, noster,* and *uester*, which are declined thus.

# DE OECONOMIA REGIA

and whatever vices there are anywhere, and the most corrupt morals, dwell, command, and reign: where the defilement, rape, adultery, and fornication of princes and nobles are but games; there also the mothers of princes and kings are sometimes the procuresses of their sons; there are the tempests of all crimes, and the unspeakable shipwreck of all virtues: every upright person is oppressed there, every worst person is promoted, the simple are mocked, the just are persecuted, the bold and impudent are raised up. Only flatterers, whisperers, detractors, tell-tales, calumniators, sycophants, liars, character-assassins, supplanters, inventors of evils, and the rest of the people of tempests flourish there, for whom all most perverse deeds are in the open: whose entire life is most base, and all of whatever most foul beastly perversity exists anywhere, all this seems to have flowed into the courtly flock as if into one body. There resides and is visited the ferocity of the lion, the cruelty of the tiger, the truculence of the bear, the rashness of the boar, the pride of the horse, the rapacity of the wolf, the obstinacy of the calf, the fraudulence of the fox, the cunning of the chameleon, the variety of the leopard, the biting nature of the dog, the desperation of the elephant, the vengeance of the camel, the timidity of the hare, the petulance of the goat, the filth of the pig, the folly of the sheep, the stupidity of the ass, the scurrility of the ape: there are raging Centaurs, there are pernicious Chimaeras, there are insane Satyrs, there are foul Harpies, there are wicked Sirens, and biformed Scyllas: there are horrid ostriches, there are voracious griffins and greedy dragons, and whatever fatal monsters and unhappy portents nature, stunted, has brought together, dwells and is seen there: there every kind of virtue suffers its own executioners and tyrants: in sum, one must either insist upon wickedness, malice, and impiety, or yield the court. It is not permitted without punishment, unless one leaves the court, who wishes to be pious. No evil can befall cities more destructive

translation: could reach, and to whom not only the open attack of enemies but not even the hidden plots of his mother could have done harm. After she came to Larinum, she who had pretended to be convinced that poison had been given to her husband by that Strato before, gave him a shop, immediately built and furnished, for the purpose of practicing medicine in Larinum. For one, two, three years Sassia remained quiet, so that she seemed to wish and hope for some calamity for her son rather than to build and plot it. Then, during the consulship of Hortensius and Metellus, in order to drag this Oppianicus—who was busy with other things and thinking nothing of this kind—into this accusation, she betrothed to him her daughter—the one she had by her son-in-law—against his will, so that, bound by the marriage and held fast by the hope of an inheritance, she might have him in her power. At almost this very time, that physician Strato committed a theft and murder in her house. Since there was a cabinet in the house in which he knew there was a fair amount of money and gold, he killed two sleeping fellow-slaves at night and threw them into the fishpond. He himself cut out the bottom of the cabinet and carried off five pounds of sesterces and gold, with the knowledge of one of the younger slaves. The theft having been discovered the next day, every suspicion was stirred up against those slaves who were not appearing. Since that cutting of the bottom of the cabinet was noticed, people were asking how it could have been done. In short, it is sought from the auctioneers, and that small saw is found to have reached Strato. If we seek what is right and just, that is quite clear: if we consult the safest and most expedient means, that is obscure and doubtful: but if we are as we ought to be, such that we consider nothing to be useful that is not just and honest, we cannot doubt what we must do.

rather looks to the degeneration of administration than to a certain form. The nature of monarchy is one thing, that of aristocracy another, that of democracy another, which, if they are mixed, extinguish each other: and different laws also befit monarchical administration, others aristocratic, others democratic, because they are different modes of administration. Hence also there arises an incurable error in the republic among those who promise that they will reform everything, because they confuse these things, as if on a stage they wish to arrange all things with one boot and one rule, when yet one shoe does not fit every foot, or one foot does not have every shoe that fits it.

4 From this it also follows that all most corrupt things follow, and the people and the republic are necessarily agitated by seditions and swords. Unless each of the three received species of a republic is preserved in its own nature, it is necessary—and it happens easily—that they collapse into their neighboring vices: monarchy has a neighboring vice, tyranny, into which it declines with little effort.

The government of the best men, or aristocracy, easily declines also into an allied vice, namely the power of the few, with the other best men expelled, just as democracy, or the authority of the whole people, declines into plebeian madness and lawless liberty. See Aristotle in the third book of the *Politics*, chapter five, and the fourth book, chapter two.

<margin>a In the epitome of his book 6.</margin> It has been observed by Polybius, most excellently, that just as rust to iron and worms or wood-borers to wood, when they mix, bring ruin, so that even if they escape all external harms, they are consumed by those things which are innate to them: in this way also to republics, for every one according to its nature, a certain peculiar malice grows and adheres. As for example a kingdom, which is monarchy among the willing, becomes tyranny; aristocracy becomes oligarchy; democracy becomes bestial, a *chaerocracy* <gloss>mob-rule</gloss> or sedition of the plebeians.

<margin>b Diogenes Laertius in the life of Plato, book 3.</margin> Plato, distributing the city or polity into five species, has encompassed the legitimate and the illegitimate or deficient republics. He says there are popular, aristocratic, oligarchic, royal, and tyrannical republics. Popular, in those cities in which the matter is acted upon according to the command of the multitude and magistrates are chosen by its nod, and laws are passed according to its judgment.

Aristocracy, or the rule of the best, where neither the rich nor the poor, nor those illustrious by nobility or glory, dominate, but those alone who are the best in the city administer the matter.

Oligarchy, when magistrates are chosen by property qualifications, for they are fewer than the poor.

5 He says a kingdom is twofold: one according to law, another according to lineage. He says the kingdom of the Carthaginians consists according to law, since it is civil; but that of the Lacedaemonians according to lineage, for they have a certain succession through lineage; but it is called a tyranny when citizens, impelled and forced by violence, are ruled by someone.

And now, when he learned that the people of Athens were in a wretched plight from famine, he sailed into the Piraeus, and reduced the city, which was compelled to make terms on the basis of his commands. It is true one hears it said by Lacedaemonians that Lysander wrote to the <term>ephors</term> <gloss>Spartan magistrates</gloss> thus: "Athens is taken"; and that the ephors wrote back to Lysander: "'Taken' were enough"; but this story was invented for its neatness' sake. The actual decree of the ephors ran thus: "This is what the Lacedaemonian authorities have decided: tear down the Piraeus and the long walls; quit all the cities and keep to your own land; if you do these things, and restore your exiles, you shall have peace, if you want it. and to exercise them in the grammatical precepts of the Greek language, when Marcus Tullius Cicero, a consular man and renowned for such great deeds performed during his consulship, was not ashamed not only to profess and show himself a master to students of eloquence, but also to dispute most subtly about syllables, oratorical rhythms, and similar matters in his *Perfect Orator*? Nor was Gaius Julius Caesar, so great and such a commander, ashamed to write most accurately on the method of speaking Latin? Nor Marcus Terentius Varro, a man, as it is agreed among all, the most learned of the Romans, to write twenty-four books on the Latin language? Nor Messalla Corvinus, the most eloquent orator after Marcus Tullius, and a most noble man, to publish entire books not only on individual words but also on letters? Lastly, of what should anyone be ashamed, unless it is shameful by its own nature? Who, however, would call it shameful for anyone to teach others what it was most honorable for him to learn, especially for free? It remains now for me to explain to you why I have decided to take up this task in this gymnasium in particular.

It does not escape you, listeners, and it is written by Marcus Tullius, that this is either implanted in us all by nature, or born of some opinion, perhaps not absurd, that when we see those places in which we know ourselves, or have heard from others, that famous men worthy of memory have walked, we are affected in a wonderful way and are moved more than if we were to hear of their deeds or read any of their writings.
